Uniform Title: Akulavīratantra Main Title: Akulavīratantram Secondary Title: Kaulajñānanirṇaya and Some Minor Texts of the School of Matsyendranātha
Author: Matsyendranātha Alternate names: Matsyendra; Macchaghaṇḍapāda (Macchagondapāda)
Editor: Bagchi, P. C.

Description: The source of this e-text is the *Calcutta Sanskrit Series* (No. 3), which contains the *Kaulajñānanirṇaya* along with several minor texts of the school of Matsyendranātha, including the *Kulānandatantra* and the *Jñānakārikā*. The printed volume also includes introductory material and summaries in English.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: August 1, 2006.
Publisher: Metropolitan Printing and Publishing House.
Publication year: 1934 Publication city: Calcutta Publication country: India
Salutations to the venerable feet of Śrīmacchanda! To the venerable Sahajānanda of the Fish, who arises from his own body,
who is the profound support of all, immovable, all-pervading, and supreme.
I bow to Mīnanātha, who is completely liberated from the impurity of illusion.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the great being Akulavīra, the secret more secret than the secret, the lineage of the true essence of the Siddhas. || 1 ||
This was spoken by Siddhanātha for the benefit of the worlds;
it should be guarded with great effort by one who desires the eternal state.
He is the great refuge for all beings submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra,
just as all rivers and streams come together in the sea.
Likewise, among the Akulavīras, all phenomena have gone to dissolution;
he is the eternal Lord, the support of the entire world without exception. (4)
Those who rely on all phenomena do not find innate bliss;
ignorant and seized by impurities, they are shrouded by the darkness of the Great Illusion.
Satisfied with the web of scriptures, they are deluded and abandon that [reality];
they do not find the peaceful state, the partless Guru of the Kaulas. (6)
Whosoever are the followers of Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika, as well as the Buddhists who are the Arhats and proponents of the Soma-siddhānta; || 7 ||
The Mīmāṃsā with its five streams, the Vāma, Siddhānta, and Dakṣiṇa [Tantras], as well as Itihāsa, Purāṇa, and the Gāruḍa which contains the reality of elemental beings; (8)

Through all these Śaiva Āgamas, which are endowed with ritual action yet remain indirect, there is the movement toward accomplishments accompanied by conceptual construction; all of that is known as the bondage of sin.
Abounding in conceptual constructions, all false doctrines are meaningless;
those who are devoid of the Akulavīra do not escape from saṃsāra. || 10 ||
Relying upon the Omniscient One, who is characterized by benefit in every respect, the accomplishment of all beings resides therein;
indeed, all accomplishment is found there.
Wherever that Akulavīra is seen facing in all directions,
having recognized him as the supreme form, the mind shall attain immobility.
Sound, form, taste, touch, and smell as the fifth—
all these states of being are dissolved and have gone to their dissolution right there.
For him whose mind consists of mind is peaceful, free from existence and non-existence, devoid of rising and setting, and considered by the wise to be the very nature of reality.
It is known as Akulavīra, the supreme support of all, both transcendent and immanent;
one should not recite the hundred-thousandfold divisions of the support within the sphere of Nāda.
It is not in the heart-center, nor in the mouth, nor in the uvula or the cavity of the palate;
there is neither the iḍā nor the piṅgalā, nor the śāntā, nor indeed any coming and going.
Nor in the navel-center or the throat, nor in the head nor indeed in the crown;
likewise not during the opening of the eyes, nor in gazing at the tip of the nose. (17)
Neither in inhalation nor in retention, nor likewise in exhalation; neither in the piercing of the *bindu*, nor in the knot at the forehead, nor in the fire. (18)
There is neither entry nor exit, neither invocation nor dismissal;
there is no ritual action (*karaṇa*), no seat, and no mudrās, for the palate is not split. (19)
There is no cessation, nor extraction, nor indeed any movement of what has passed;
there is neither the impelled nor the impeller, nor a location, nor even a support.
Nor can that state which transcends the graspable be grasped by the self alone;
it is free from such positions and devoid of logical reasons or examples.
Within that, both the external and internal, as well as all that is moving and unmoving, exist as a single utterance.
Neither far nor indeed near, neither full nor empty; it is not high, nor is it excessive—it is devoid of these attributes.
That person (pudgala) who indeed consists of these twenty [elements] does not exist;
where no characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is found, he is called the Akulavīra. || 23 ||
He for whom [this] is thus established, who abides in the state of equal flavor—he is Brahmā, he is Hari, he is Īśa, he is Rudra, and he is Īśvara. || 24 ||
He is Śiva, the supreme deity; he is likewise Soma, Arka, and Agni. He is Sāṃkhya and the Purāṇas, as well as the Arhat and the Buddha. (25)
The Goddess herself, the God himself, the disciple himself, the teacher himself;
meditation itself, the meditator himself—the deity is everywhere himself. (26)
Whatever state of being a person constantly cultivates, he obtains a corresponding fruit; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (27)
For indeed, the names of this very [reality] are proclaimed separately by yogins who are deluded by erroneous cognition; yet it is sung of as being nameless. (28)
Afflicted by both merit and demerit, and shrouded by the darkness of non-conceptualization, they therefore abandon cyclic existence, which is crowded with various wombs and hells. (29)
When they behold the great being Akulavīra, who is omnipresent,
he is eternally of a single form within and without, comprising all that is moving and unmoving. (30)
It is waveless, without appearance, devoid of distinctions of state,
free from all limbs or parts, without dissolution, and born of no modification.
Unseen, devoid of qualities, peaceful, transcending all principles, stainless, omniscient, perfectly complete, and its very nature is thus imperishable.
Free from cause and effect, inconceivable, and free from affliction;
beyond illusion, without support, all-pervading, and facing every direction. || 33 ||
It is equanimity and a single entity, devoid of conjecture and exclusion;
it is the great being Akulavīra, free from existence and non-existence. || 34 ||
Neither mind, nor intellect, nor thought, nor consciousness and so forth;
neither time, nor the power of calculation, nor Śiva, nor the senses. (35)
For that which has arisen is not grasped, nor is it indeed pleasure or pain;
for there is no taste, nor is it indeed pleasure or pain. || 36 ||
It has neither taste nor lack of taste, it is neither created nor born;
it has neither shadow nor heat, and it is neither cold nor hot.
There, my mind is seen to be free from rising and setting;
no boundary is seen there, nor indeed any sectarian path. 38.
Non-dual, immovable, peaceful, and free from the defects of attachment;
undisturbed, free from conceptual construction, and bound by the characteristics of impurity. || 39 ||
It is without protector and yet the protector of all; it is the state beyond the mind (unmanā), free from intoxication;
it is neither concealed nor joined together; it is both the stationary and the moving. || 40 ||
And by the stage of the blazing fire, as well as by water, everything is filled with equal flavor; it is solely the Akulavīra. (41)
He for whom this liberation is firmly established is liberated from the bonds of existence;
for him there is neither mother nor father, nor kinsman, nor deity.
Having abandoned sacrifice, fasting, ritual action, and the distinctions of caste,
and having cast off the multitude of conceptual constructions, they have gone to the dissolution in the Akula-vīra.
There is no recitation, no worship, no bathing, no fire-oblation, and no spiritual practice;
there is no entering the fire, nor is there the hurling of oneself from a cliff during the winter.
He has no fixed rule, nor is fasting prescribed for him;
he does not perform rites for the ancestors, nor the vows of pilgrimage. (45)
There is no fruit of merit or demerit; there is neither ritual bathing nor water-rites.
Abandon yourself from all activities, including those that are the customs of the world. (46)

Those who have performed the rituals of the Samaya conduct, those bound by vows, as well as those with conceptualization and discursive thought, and others who are indeed practitioners of dharma—[all these are included]. (47)
In this state, the yogi is without conventional conduct and is free from the behavior of the uninitiated;
he attains various forms of accomplishment as well as the elixir of immortality in the netherworld.
And whatever is directly perceived, one should never fail to grasp;
for the entire web of fetters is that which leads one down the lower path. (49)
Among these, there is no liberation for those who are devoid of the *akula-vīra*;
just as the dead do not perceive the taste of the bitter or the sweet. (50)
Likewise, they do not know the Akulavīra, which is accessible through its own nature;
it is like wine for a great man, which cannot be described for one who is not worthy. 51.
Pages 89 to 96 are missing.
(Page 97) This supreme bliss of the secret is extremely hidden and well-guarded.
And for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, it was spoken by Siddhanātha. || 39 ||
The state beyond conceptual construction is peaceful, wherein both the supreme and the non-supreme are dissolved;
that is the great abode of liberation, devoid of the form of mantra.
In that very state, having gone forth in the form of creation, she returns there again to dissolution; what is the use of saying more? [It is] entirely free from all bonds.
When Akulavīra has been attained, what then is the use of Kaulika sequences?
For having attained Akulavīra, which is the true essence of liberation and the remover of impurities, [what further is needed]? 42.
In the Kaula path, there are two [types of Kuṇḍalinī]: the artificial and likewise the innate.
The artificial is to be known as Kuṇḍalinī; the innate abides in the state of equal flavor (samarasa).
That [state] which exists as the relationship between the impelled and the impeller is called "the created" (kṛtakā).
Then, by means of the mudrās and mantras employed, he should cause it to fall to the ground. (44)
Others [attain it] through the falling of oblations, by the muttering of the ear-vidyā, and with incense;
this is the goal to be accomplished, this is the reality, as well as meditation and concentration.
Through many accumulations of karma and the cultivation of various paths, those of deluded minds are bewildered, tossed by the surging waves of conceptual construction. (46)
Her heart was tormented by grief, and due to her attachment, she was filled with great fears;
overcome by both joy and despair, she was lamenting again and again. (47)
For so long they wander through the ocean of existence for eons upon eons;
yet, just as growth does not arise from burnt seeds, so too rebirth no longer occurs.
Just as no new growth is found in a tree whose roots have been severed, so too that which has entered the state of the Akulavīra is severed from the bonds of various worldly existences. 49.
Just as mercury that has reached dissolution is not bound when it is pure,
so too [is he not bound] when he has entered the state called *bhrāma* within the *sattva* of the *Kulavīra*. (50)
Just as one does not see the risen sun when it is shrouded by darkness, so too, due to ignorance of the mind, one is deluded by the web of errors. 51.
When the Akula and Vīra [states] are attained, all this perishes, just as clarified butter exists within curd, or as fire resides within wood. 52.
As fragrance resides in a flower, oil in sesame seeds, shade in a tree, joy within wine, and radiance in a lamp, so [does it reside within]. 53.
And within the lotus, the limbs and sub-limbs of Kuṇḍalī, as well as all that belongs to the Raktārtha-Ākulavīra, are likewise assigned there. (54)
Those whose minds are deluded by artificial things do not know Akulavīra through cognitive objects associated with existence, non-existence, and the like, which fall within the range of vision. 55.
Bound by the net of snares and deluded by great illusion, they do not know the peaceful state, which is inconceivable and eternally manifest. 56.

Abiding in the state that pervades all, devoid of place and color, it dwells within all beings; indeed, it is the one that is to be meditated upon, yet is itself free from being an object of meditation. || 57 ||
And that all-pervading reality is stable, full, and continuous;
therein the mind dissolves, becoming motionless and absorbed in that. (58)
The expansion of the mind, when thus contemplated and cast [into that state], attains identity with it;
it remains established in reality within the partless and imperishable Śiva.
Then one attains identity with that, the stainless and immovable state—the great wonder, the Akulavīra, the solitary hero who is omnipresent. (60)
Difficult to attain is this sphere of experience for gods, *siddhas*, and *yoginīs*.
Some say, "This is the Dharma," "This is the scripture," or "This is the austerity. (61)
This is the world, this is heaven, this is what is to be accomplished, and this is the fruit;
this is knowledge and realized wisdom, and this is the supreme purity and impurity.
When the knowable, the peak of reality, and therein both meditation and retention are present, then that yoginī is indeed one; there is no other, for there is no second.
Neither that which has not yet come nor that which has already gone moves, nor does it stand still;
it is neither past nor future, and is devoid of both persistence and dissolution.
And I am never defiled by accumulated faults;
I am no one, nor does anyone belong to me; I am neither bound, nor is there any binder.
He is neither unliberated nor is there non-liberation for him; he has no longing even for liberation.
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, eating, or even in sexual union—66.
One should never perform medical treatment for fear, poverty, grief, various kinds of consumption, nor for the sake of the objects of the senses.
He may associate with all castes, yet he should not discriminate regarding what is fit to be eaten;
thus that yogi conducts himself, like a fire in the forest. 68.
There is no state of various bondages of the *piṇḍa* for one with the tendencies of a fool;
likewise, it is devoid of the Moon and Fire, and abandoned by breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). (69)
It is immeasurable and free from appearances, devoid of dhāraṇī and dhyāna;
by him through whom the Guru has been worshipped with devotion for thousands of births. (70)
Those who possess unwavering devotion to the circle of the Yoginīs and Rākiṇīs obtain great wisdom and the liberation granted by the Akulavīra. (71)
The Akulavīra is the great being, profound and of impenetrable nature;
when it is known as that which transcends the body, it is bodiless and devoid of any physical form.
Free from words and syllables, stainless and eternally manifest—by being absorbed in that, one whose self is identical with it attains the eternal state. (73)
For he would indeed transcend thought, being free from the application of yoga;
he is Nirvana, devoid of latent impressions, a self-satisfied soul, and free from all affliction.
By him, without a doubt, those stainless [realities] that cut through impurity have been attained;
for him alone does that which is all-pervading quickly manifest.
The various scriptures of Vedic tenets and the Śikhins—all these are delusions, leading only to the useless exhaustion of the body. (76)
Seized by the pride of learning, they are arrogant and have gone to an evil state;
satisfied with what is worthless, they contemplate the meaning of many books. (77)
Those whose minds are deluded by artificial constructs do not find the Akulavīra;
how can there be knowledge for the arrogant, even through hundreds of millions of books? (78)
Camphor, saffron, and the like, as well as clothing and betel—
[if he treats these] like a donkey carrying a load, all that is for him utterly useless.
And when one perceives the Akulavīra residing within the body as all-pervading, || 79 ||
In the ritual section [of the Veda], there is no fruit of dharma or adharma, nor is there water from visiting sacred fords;
there is neither ritual action, truth, nor purity, nor is there meditative cultivation.
For him, there are neither actions nor non-actions, nor worldly customs;
he has practiced the conduct of the *samaya* as it is followed by people deluded by error. (81)
They do not know the Akulavīra; what is its excellence, and where does it abide?
In this world, bonds are artificial and imagined by wicked scholars. (82)
Volition and doubt, as well as the various arts and actions, the diverse supernatural powers in the world, the netherworld, and elixirs—[all these arise from that]. (83)
And when that which is directly perceived is obtained, one should never reject it;
all those who do so are bound by fetters and are givers of the downward path. 84.
And by these [means], there is no liberation from saṃsāra; for those devoid of heroes, the family lineage is lost, just as the intoxicating bliss described does not arise at all. 85.
In the same way, foolish men do not know that which is called the Akulavīra, the supreme instruction to be personally realized, which is the most essential of all essentials. 86.
The self remains deluded by error only so long as it does not find its foundation;
when the yogi [rests] in that which transcends thought, he is a yogi who contemplates yoga.

He whose latent impressions have become dispassionate, whose soul is satisfied, and who is free from affliction—only so long do those of deluded nature wander, bound by the attachments to various states of existence. (88)
As long as one does not find the equality and oneness that is supreme bliss, it is like the sexual pleasure of fools according to the scriptures, or like that of a maiden. (89)
The young maidens find the Akulavīra through these explanations—[a reality] liberated from the directions and locations, and devoid of places and phonemes. (90)
Unconfused, free from conceptual construction, devoid of qualities, and perfectly pure;
without protector yet the protector of all, and free from negligence and madness. || 91 ||
In things dense and compact, in those with loose joints, and in all that is stationary as well as moving; likewise in water, fire, wind, earth, and space. (92)
That which is everywhere of equal flavor, filled, and the unique Akulavīra—by whomsoever that is known as residing within the body, he is liberated from all bonds. 93.
For him there is no bondage of action, no object of knowledge, and no sensation;
there is no sacrifice, no fasting, no conduct, and no arising of ritual activity. (94)
There is no caste nor distinction of caste when one has arrived at the Akulavīra;
there is no recitation, no worship, no sacred fires, no burnt offering, and indeed no ritual means of accomplishment.

For him, there is no requirement for entering fire, nor for the performance of mantra-recitation, worship, or ritual ablutions; nor does he have any observances regarding the service of sacred fields and seats.
There is no ritual action, nor worship, nor sacred fords, nor vows;
it is the supportless state, peaceful, transcendent, and stainless.
It is perceived as being complete with omniscience by its very nature;
it is free from cause and effect, inconceivable, and untainted.
Beyond illusion, without support, all-pervading, and facing every direction;
established within one's own body, peaceful—that is called Akulavīra. 99.
All has become one at once, devoid of the absence of duality;
it is the great being, Akulavīra, free from existence and non-existence. || 100 ||
The mind, intellect, consciousness, and that which is beyond consciousness have no self-awareness; there is neither the measurement of time, nor power, nor the sense faculties. (101)
It is not perceived in the elements, for it is neither suffering nor even pleasure;
it is neither taste nor superior taste, neither the produced nor the producer. 102.
There is neither shadow nor sunlight, neither fire nor the sensation of cold or heat;
it is said to be without day or night, devoid of rising and setting. (103)
Therein the mind is not seen, nor is anything above or middle known;
such is the determination of reality—unshakeable, immovable, and peaceful. (104)
Whatever state of being a person constantly cultivates, he obtains a corresponding fruit; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (105)
And thus, why do those deluded by erroneous cognition seek to reach that which is the true nature of the family, the ineffable supreme nectar, which is unattainable? (106)
Neither distant nor near, neither perceptible nor imperceptible;
neither full nor empty, neither subtle nor excessive. (107)
This [teaching] is free from partisan positions and devoid of logical reasons and examples;
it is for those deluded by artificial constructs, the ignorant who are devoted solely to the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa). 108.
There is no liberation for them in saṃsāra, in hell, or amidst the confusion of wombs;
rather, when they behold the all-pervading Akulavīra, the great being. || 109 ||
The unity of the internal and external is established everywhere;
it is without waves, without appearance, and free from the fragmentation of words. 110.
It is devoid of all limbs, changeless, stainless, invisible, free from qualities, eternal, unobstructed, and immovable. || 111 ||
There is no meditation, nor indeed retention, nor posture, nor even color; there is no exhaling, nor inhaling, nor the upward stroke (*udghāta*), nor the breath-retention (*kumbhaka*). (112)

It exists neither at the end, the beginning, nor in the middle; it is not the growth of what already exists; it is free from the grasped and the grasper, and it is that which transcends all knots. || 113 ||
Completely liberated from all these, devoid of causes and examples, it is established everywhere as the oneness of both the internal and the external. (114)

Those who have realized the Great Being, Akulavīra, who resides within their own body, as being of a single form throughout the moving and the unmoving by way of the bliss of the equal flavor (samarasānanda). || 115 ||
He under whose control some person remains, established in the state of equal flavor (samarasa), he is indeed Brahmā, he is Hari, he is Rudra, and likewise Īśvara. (116)
He is the eternal god Śiva, and he is Soma, Arka, and Śaṅkara;
he is Viśākha, Mayūrākṣa, Arhat, and indeed Budha. (117)
The Goddess herself, the God himself, the disciple himself, and the teacher himself;
meditation itself, the meditator himself—the teacher is the Lord of All himself. (118)
The Omniscient One, having pervaded all, is characterized by benefit in every respect;
all Yoginīs reside there, and indeed all the Siddhas are present there as well. (119)
Everything therein is indeed for all purposes and possesses all-knowledge;
because it is of great significance, it is known as Akulavīra.
Sound, touch, taste, form, smell, and the [objects of] the ears and hands—all these are fearful; they are dissolved right there, having gone to their dissolution. (121)
Neither in the support, nor in the object of meditation, nor in the supreme sphere of sound (nāda);
neither in the heart, nor in the navel, the throat, the mouth, or the two cavities of the uvula. || 122 ||
Neither the iḍā, nor the piṅgalā, nor the suṣumṇā exist through coming and going; they do not exist in the navel-wheel, nor in the throat, nor likewise in the head or the bindu. (123)
There is no opening of the eyes or ears in this way when gazing at the tip of the nose, nor during inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), or exhalation (recaka). || 124 ||
There is no division of the *bindu* in the knot on the forehead, nor is there a moon;
likewise, during inhalation and exhalation, the crest-lock (*śikhā*) is not located above the *bindu*.

Not by hand gestures, nor by arrows, nor by mudrās; not in the sky, nor in the circle of wind; not in the bow, nor in the moon and sun, nor in existence and non-existence, nor in their union. || 126 ||
It is incomparable, without support, and free from both sides and their opposites;
yet those whose souls are seized by the impurity of ignorance are utterly deluded by the great māyā.

Those whose minds are deluded by the literal meaning of the scriptures, even though they are learned people, do not know the peaceful state—the teacherless, actionless state of absolute liberation (kaivalya). || 128 ||

And whoever there may be—the followers of Saṃkhya and others, as well as the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas; the Buddhists and Arhats, and those who follow the Soma-siddhānta and the Dakṣiṇā-path. || 129 ||
Mīmāṃsā, Pañcarātra, Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, and Kaulika; the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, Bhūtatattva, and Gāruḍa. || 130 ||
All these are indeed equal, or some are endowed with ritual action; all grant the accomplishment of one's conceptual constructs, yet those who know them are not truly wise.
All those who are full of conceptual constructions and whose speech is false and meaningless are not liberated from saṃsāra, being devoid of the heroes of the [spiritual] family. 132.
Whatever places there may be— mountains, cities, and oceans—
it is eternally present everywhere, both in the immobile and in the mobile.
Everything whatsoever that exists, moving or unmoving, consists of the five elements;
from Śiva down to the lowest gods, all are established therein. (134)
Seeing such a yogin, those men who approach him with perfumes, flowers, incense, and various foods and drinks— || 135 ||

And those devotees who satisfy [the deity] with the three kinds [of offerings] from within their inner self, they too are liberated from bonds, even if they do not desire the path to liberation. || 136 ||
Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as the Arhat and the Buddha;
those known as Viṣa and Mayūrākṣa, and the sages whose wealth is their asceticism. || 137 ||
Kings, gods, and others who desire liberation—all of them seek liberation; yet it is Akulavīra alone who bestows liberation. 138.
Now I shall explain another [teaching] concerning the state of differentiation for one who abides in the essential nature;
that which was previously stated by all [the teachers] pertains to the path of lineage (*anvayamārga*) within the non-kaulika system. (139)
They are completely satisfied by the supreme nectar and possess only innate bliss. || 140 ||
For them there is no old age, nor death, nor grief, nor even suffering;
it removes all diseases and there is no further occurrence of rebirth. || 141 ||
The divine Akulavīra abides by the grace of Siddhanātha;
he is pure in every respect and at all times, and he is the Lord in every respect and at all times. (142)
Thus ends the Akulavīra, obtained through the grace of the Yoginī at the site of Kāmarūpa, as brought down by the feet of Macchendra.
